why.body:
The CPU can only run what is in main memory, and that memory is shared by the OS and every process, so someone must manage it, and you can see why from four separate worries. A CPU can run only what is in main memory, and main memory is shared by the OS and by every running process. The memory manager has four jobs. Relocation: a program cannot know in advance where in RAM it will be loaded, so its addresses must be translated. Protection: one process must not read or write another’s memory, nor the kernel’s. Sharing: sometimes processes should share (library code, shared memory). Organisation: memory must be used efficiently, with little wasted and the ability to run programs larger than RAM.

The key idea behind every scheme is the distinction between a logical (virtual) address — the address the program generates — and a physical address — the actual location in RAM. The hardware memory-management unit (MMU) translates one into the other on every memory reference. Because translation happens at run time, the OS can move a program in memory, give it non-contiguous pieces, and even keep only part of it resident. “Address binding” can happen at compile time (absolute code, rare), load time (relocatable code fixed when loaded) or, in modern systems, execution time (the MMU).

The simplest MMU is a pair of registers: base and limit. Every logical address is compared with the limit (a protection check) and added to the base to give the physical address. Switching processes means loading different base/limit values — nothing else is needed to isolate them.

Match each job, relocation, protection, sharing and organisation, to a problem you would meet if two programs ran at once. Which job stops one program reading another’s data?
keynotes: A CPU can run only what is in main memory, which the OS and every running process share.
The memory manager has four jobs: relocation, protection, sharing and organisation.
Relocation is needed because a program cannot know in advance where in RAM it will be loaded, so its addresses must be translated.

alloc.body:
The simplest scheme gives each process one block of memory in a single piece, and you will see how even that simple idea leaves wasted gaps. The simplest scheme gives each process one contiguous block of physical memory. Early systems cut memory into fixed partitions, which wastes the unused part of each partition (internal fragmentation). Later systems use variable partitions: the OS keeps a list of free holes and, for each request, chooses one. First fit takes the first hole big enough (fast); best fit takes the smallest hole that fits (leaves the smallest leftover, but scans the whole list and tends to create tiny useless slivers); worst fit takes the largest (leaves a big remainder, but destroys the large holes). Simulation studies show first fit and best fit beat worst fit in storage use, with first fit usually faster.

Whatever is left over is too small to use — external fragmentation. Statistically, for first fit about one third of memory ends up unusable (the “50 % rule”: for every N allocated blocks about N/2 are lost to fragmentation). Compaction squeezes all the holes into one by moving processes, but it needs run-time relocation and costs a great deal of copying. Paging, next, removes the problem at its root. Run the three cards: the same requests are placed very differently.

Place requests of 212, 417, 112 and 426 KB into holes using first fit and best fit. Which leaves the tiniest useless fragments?
keynotes: Early systems cut memory into fixed partitions, which wastes the unused part of each (internal fragmentation).
Variable partitions keep a list of free holes: first fit takes the first hole big enough, best fit takes the smallest hole that fits.
The scattered leftovers are external fragmentation.

paging.body:
Here is the idea that removed the fragmentation problem almost entirely: cut memory into equal pieces, so that any piece fits anywhere, and you will see why it works. Paging cuts the virtual address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size frames. Any page can go in any frame, so external fragmentation disappears; only the last page of a process wastes part of a frame (internal fragmentation, on average half a page). A per-process page table maps page number → frame number. A virtual address of m bits with page size 2n splits into a page number (the top m − n bits) and an offset (the low n bits); the offset passes through unchanged because pages and frames are the same size.

With 4 KB pages (n = 12), the address 0x3A7C has page number 3 and offset 0xA7C; if page 3 lives in frame 9, the physical address is 9·4096 + 0xA7C. The page table entry also carries valid (is the page in memory?), protection (read/write/execute), dirty (modified?) and referenced bits — the hooks for protection and for replacement.

Where does the page table live? In main memory — which means each reference costs two memory accesses: one for the page-table entry, one for the data. To avoid the doubling, the MMU has a small, fast associative cache of recent translations, the TLB (translation look-aside buffer). A TLB hit gives the frame in one fast step; a miss walks the table and loads the entry. Because programs show locality, hit ratios of 98–99 % are normal. The effective access time is a weighted average, worked below and tabulated in the figure.

Split the virtual address 0x1A3F into page number and offset for 4 KB pages. Which part is translated, and which is copied unchanged?
keynotes: Paging cuts the virtual address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size frames, so external fragmentation disappears.
Only the last page of a process wastes part of a frame (internal fragmentation, on average half a page).
A per-process page table maps page number to frame number, and the offset passes through unchanged.

multilevel.body:
A flat page table can be monstrous, and the cure, which you know from the index of a book, is to page the page table itself. A flat page table can be enormous. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2²⁰ pages; at 4 bytes per entry the table is 4 MB per process, most of it describing addresses the process never uses. On a 64-bit machine a flat table is impossible. The standard cure is a hierarchical (multilevel) page table: page the page table itself. A 32-bit address is split 10 + 10 + 12: the first 10 bits index an outer table whose entries point to inner tables, the next 10 bits index the inner table, and the last 12 are the offset. Inner tables for unused regions simply do not exist, so a small process uses a handful of tables. The price is more memory accesses per translation on a TLB miss (one per level), which the TLB hides.

An alternative is the inverted page table: one entry per physical frame, recording which (process, page) occupies it. Its size depends on RAM, not on address-space size, which suits 64-bit machines, but looking up a page means searching the table — made fast with a hash on (pid, page number). Sharing pages between processes is harder in this scheme.

Work out the size of a flat table for 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, then explain why splitting it 10 + 10 + 12 saves memory.
keynotes: With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2²⁰ pages, so a flat table at 4 bytes per entry is 4 MB per process.
A multilevel table splits a 32-bit address as 10 + 10 + 12, with the first 10 bits indexing an outer table whose entries point to inner tables.
Inverted page tables keep one entry per physical frame instead.

seg.body:
Paging splits memory by size, but you think in terms of meaning: code here, data there, stack somewhere else, and segmentation follows that view. Paging splits memory by size; segmentation divides a program by meaning — code, data, stack, each library — as a programmer thinks of it. An address is a pair (segment, offset); a segment table holds each segment’s base and limit, and an offset beyond the limit is a protection fault. Segments are visible to the programmer and variable-sized, so they bring back external fragmentation and a more complicated allocation problem, but they make protection and sharing natural: a code segment can be marked read-only and shared by many processes, a stack segment can grow independently.

Real systems combine both ideas. Intel’s early x86 used segmentation; modern 64-bit systems use a flat model with paging. A paged segment scheme splits each segment into pages, so segments give meaningful protection while pages give fixed-size allocation.

What is the difference between a segment and a page, and why does segmentation bring external fragmentation back?
keynotes: Segmentation divides a program by meaning, such as code, data, stack and each library.
An address is a pair (segment, offset); a segment table holds each segment’s base and limit, and an offset beyond the limit is a protection fault.
Segments are variable-sized, so they bring back external fragmentation.

virtual.body:
Why load a whole program when most of it, such as error handlers, never runs? Virtual memory exploits that fact, and you can think of it as lazy loading done properly. Why load a whole program when most of it — error handlers, rarely used features — never runs? Virtual memory separates the programmer’s view of memory from the physical reality: a program may be larger than RAM because only the pages actually in use need be resident, the rest living on disk (the swap area or the executable itself). With demand paging a page is brought in only when it is first referenced. Each page-table entry has a valid bit; if it is clear, the reference triggers a page fault.

Handling a page fault takes a dozen steps, and the figure walks through them: the MMU traps to the OS; the OS checks that the reference is legal (otherwise it kills the process); it finds a free frame (or evicts one); it schedules a disk read and switches to another process while waiting; when the read completes it updates the page table and ready queue; finally it restarts the faulting instruction, which now succeeds. The instruction is restarted from scratch, which is why the hardware must be able to undo a half-finished instruction.

A fault costs milliseconds against nanoseconds for a normal access — a factor of tens of thousands — so even a tiny fault rate hurts. The effective access time is EAT = (1 − p)·m + p·F, where p is the fault probability, m the memory access time and F the fault service time. The worked example turns this into a requirement on p.

Trace a page fault step by step: trap, find the page on disk, pick a frame, read it in, update the page table, restart. Which step is slowest?
keynotes: Virtual memory separates the programmer’s view of memory from the physical reality, so a program may be larger than RAM.
With demand paging a page is brought in only when it is first referenced.
Each page-table entry has a valid bit, and touching an absent page causes a page fault.

replace.body:
When no frame is free the OS must throw a page out, and the whole art is to evict the one that will be needed furthest in the future, which you can only guess. If a fault occurs and no frame is free, the OS must evict a page. The goal of every policy is to evict the page that will be needed furthest in the future. FIFO evicts the oldest resident page — trivially cheap, but it may throw out a heavily used page just because it arrived early. LRU evicts the least recently used page, using the past as a predictor of the future (locality of reference). The unreachable optimal policy evicts the page needed furthest ahead; it needs the future so it cannot be built, but it is the yardstick every algorithm is measured against. LFU evicts the least frequently used page.

Exact LRU is expensive (a timestamp or a stack update on every reference), so real kernels approximate it. The second-chance (clock) algorithm keeps pages in a circular list with a reference bit: the hand sweeps; a page with bit 1 gets the bit cleared and a second chance, a page with bit 0 is evicted. Enhanced versions consider the dirty bit too, preferring clean pages (no write-back needed). Pages are also evicted in the background so a free frame is waiting at fault time.

On the textbook reference string with 3 frames: FIFO = 15 faults, LRU = 12, optimal = 9 of 20 references. The cards animate each: red marks a fault, green a hit.

Run FIFO and LRU on a short reference string and compare the fault counts. Which policy uses the past to predict the future?
keynotes: The goal of every policy is to evict the page that will be needed furthest in the future.
FIFO evicts the oldest resident page, cheap but it may throw out a heavily used page; LRU evicts the least recently used page, using locality of reference.
The optimal policy is unreachable but serves as a yardstick.

belady.body:
More frames should always mean fewer faults, shouldn’t they? For FIFO they do not, and you can see the surprise for yourself. More frames should mean fewer faults — but not for FIFO. On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, three frames give 9 faults and four frames give 10: Belady's anomaly. It happens because FIFO’s resident set with n frames is not always a subset of its resident set with n + 1 frames, so the extra frame can change which pages are present at the wrong moment. Algorithms for which the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of that with n + 1 frames — LRU and optimal — are called stack algorithms and cannot show the anomaly.

Run both cards below and compare the fault counts. The lesson is subtle: the anomaly is rare in practice, but it destroys the intuition that adding memory can only help, and it is the standard exam question on why FIFO is a poor policy.

Count the faults on the string with three frames and with four frames. Why does LRU never behave this way?
keynotes: On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, three frames give 9 faults and four frames give 10: Belady’s anomaly.
It happens because FIFO’s resident set with n frames is not always a subset of its resident set with n + 1 frames.
Algorithms for which the set with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1, such as LRU, are free of it.

thrash.body:
Give each process too few frames and the system spends all its time swapping and none of it working, a failure you may have felt when a computer grinds to a halt. With several processes, how many frames should each get? Equal allocation gives m/n frames to each of n processes; proportional allocation gives each a share proportional to its size. Replacement can be local (a process evicts only its own pages — predictable but may starve) or global (any frame may be taken — better throughput but one process can hurt another).

Thrashing is the failure mode. A process needs a minimum number of frames to make progress — its working set, the pages it has referenced in the last Δ references. If it has fewer frames than its working set, it faults continually; the processes queue at the disk; the CPU, seeing low utilisation, admits more processes (the long-term scheduler thinks it should raise multiprogramming), which steal even more frames — a vicious circle in which utilisation collapses. The cure is to measure the working sets (or the page-fault frequency) and, when the total demand exceeds memory, to suspend some processes entirely rather than slow all of them.

Say in your own words why adding more processes can make CPU utilisation fall once thrashing starts. What would you do to stop it?
keynotes: Equal allocation gives m/n frames to each of n processes; proportional allocation gives each a share proportional to its size.
Local replacement is predictable but may starve a process; global replacement gives better throughput but one process can hurt another.
Thrashing occurs when a process lacks its minimum number of frames and spends its time faulting.

summary.body:
Here is the chapter in short form, and you can use it as a checklist before the exam.

  • Logical addresses are translated to physical ones by the MMU on every reference; base/limit is the simplest scheme.
  • Contiguous allocation suffers external fragmentation (first/best/worst fit); paging removes it, with a page table mapping page → frame and the offset unchanged.
  • The TLB hides the page-table cost: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m). Multilevel and inverted tables shrink the table.
  • Segmentation matches program structure; real systems combine segments and pages.
  • Demand paging loads on first reference; EAT = (1 − p)m + pF, so p must be tiny.
  • Optimal ≤ LRU ≲ FIFO on real programs; FIFO can even get worse with more frames (Belady); clock approximates LRU.
  • Thrashing = fewer frames than the working set; cure by suspending processes.

Recite the effective access time formula and explain each term, then check it against the summary.
keynotes: The MMU translates logical to physical addresses on every reference; paging removes external fragmentation.
The TLB hides the page-table cost: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m).
Multilevel and inverted tables shrink the page table; segmentation matches program structure.
